en: Verses in Praise of the Dharmadhātu,
composed by the Holy Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna at the Indrasabhā Monastery in the kingdom of Udḍiyāna, North India.
I take refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions— The Dharmakāya, as well as the Saṃbhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya.
May I, together with all sentient beings, Swiftly realize the nature of the Dharmadhātu.
Though we wander through the three evil realms, The principle of the Dharmadhātu remains eternally still.
Primordially and eternally pure, it cannot be altered by any marks;
Tranquil like space, it pervades everywhere;
Its essence is free from both "this" and "that," Neither deep nor shallow.
While the milk has not yet been transformed, the ghee and clarified butter (maṇḍa) are not seen;
as long as the afflictions have not been subdued and eliminated, the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) has no means of manifesting.
Just as when ghee resides within milk, the ghee is inherently wondrous, luminous, and pure.
The dharma-realm is shrouded by afflictions, yet its perfect essence is pure.
Just as a lamp obstructed by barriers cannot illuminate other things, so too,
when the mind is constantly covered by ignorance, the dharma-realm is not clearly perceived.
Just as a lamp, free from obstructions, can illuminate objects everywhere,
so too when the afflictions are destroyed, True Suchness (tathatā) is ever-manifest.
At the beginning, middle, and end, it cannot be disturbed by the two obstacles.
Like a pure lapis lazuli gem, which constantly radiates light;
though its brilliance is obstructed by other objects, the light itself is not seen when so obscured.
Thus, when the dharma-realm is shrouded by afflictions, the principle of suchness is difficult to manifest.
The essence of parinirvāṇa is pure and radiant; saṃsāra cannot defile it.
Diligently seeking to enter the dharmadhātu, saṃsāra cannot obscure it.
Just as when rice is enveloped by husks, the substance of the grain is not absent within the rice.
Afflictions veil the True Suchness, yet True Suchness exists within afflictions;
just as when the husk is removed from grain, the essence of the rice naturally appears, so too,
when one is freed from the husk of afflictions, the principle of the Dharma-realm is finally revealed.
The false attachment that a world exists is like the plantain tree, which ultimately has no core;
the Dharma-realm is not a world, nor is it a false vision.
Like a person drinking nectar, all feverish afflictions are entirely removed.
If one realizes the nature of the dharmadhātu, all the fevers of affliction are cast away.
When the flames of affliction are extinguished, the nectar of the dharmadhātu appears;
among all sentient beings, high and low are entirely equal.
In its true essence, the fruit is not produced; one clings to the seed and the fruit as non-existent.
When wisdom arises, conditioned phenomena are no longer the dharma-realm.
The dharma-realm has no location from the beginning; it is only through ultimate realization that it can be witnessed.
Pure and eternally radiant, the sun and moon are both crystalline and clear.
The Dharma-realm is free from defilement, like dust swept away by a dragon’s night rain;
how much more so when compared to the face of Rāhu—its light remains ever resplendent.
It is like fire-washed cloth: dwelling in the fire, it is able to leave behind its stains;
once the grime is removed, the cloth remains, its radiance becoming even more brilliant and pure.
So too, craving defiles the mind, and through delusion there is saṃsāra.
It is also like fire-washed cloth: in true emptiness, delusion does not exist.
The three poisons are the root of birth and death; the fire of wisdom can burn them away.
The essence of the dharma-realm is eternally present, shining brightly and constantly illuminating.
The afflictions, being defiled, are called "stains," as the World-Honored One has constantly proclaimed;
when the stains are extinguished, True Suchness (tathatā) is revealed, like drawing a spring from within the earth.
The essence of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is inherently stainless, yet the root and secondary afflictions are able to conceal it.
If afflictions are completely eliminated, One is pure and beyond measure.
The Dharma-realm is fundamentally without self, Nor the two genders, male or female;
When the essence is free from false attachments, Where is there anything left to contemplate?
The Dharma-realm is free from hatred and love; the faculties, objects, and spheres are fundamentally non-existent.
Through false attachment, they are grasped as causes, and from this, differentiation arises.
True emptiness is not suffering; craving and attachment are the cause of suffering.
Attachment arises from false conceptualization; thus one revolves through the three realms.
While the fetus dwells within the womb, the infant has not yet spoken or seen;
so too, when the two obscurations veil True Suchness (Tathatā), one cannot realize the Dharma-realm (Dharmadhātu).
Various doubts and suspicions arise; through views, pride, hatred, and delusion, one falsely imagines the unreal to be real, and the real to be non-existent.
The essence of a rabbit’s horn does not exist, yet false attachment causes it to appear as real.
The dharma-realm is free from false attachment; in false attachment, reality does not exist.
Just as form must be destroyed, its subtle particles can still be known;
but the dharma-realm is not subject to destruction, for it cannot be found throughout the three times.
Birth is followed by cessation, and honor and disgrace likewise follow one another;
yet the Dharma-realm is neither born nor extinguished—how can it be said to be an object of knowledge?
A rabbit’s horn is fundamentally non-existent, yet one may still conceive of it across the three periods of time.
True emptiness is not like a hare’s horn; it cannot be known through discursive thought.
True emptiness is called the Sugata; all marks of form have utterly vanished.
Manifestations appear according to conditions; by cultivating causes, one leaves behind attachment and error.
Perfectly pervasive like the sun and moon, The reflections they cast in water are all alike;
When form and sound are both utterly extinguished, How can there be any distinction?
The three periods of time may be investigated, And the conditions for birth are determined by time.
If one awakens to the nature of one's own body, how can that body truly exist?
Like water dwelling at the edge of heat, when it encounters heat, one perceives it as non-existent;
the principle is the same at the edge of cold—perfect penetration is always thus.
The mind is constantly shrouded by afflictions, Deluded and unable to comprehend;
If one is freed from the entanglements of affliction, One awakens to the fact that [phenomena] do not exist.
Just as the eye perceives various forms, It can illuminate clearly when free from obstructions.
The principle of true emptiness is likewise: its radiance is free from arising and ceasing.
When the auditory consciousness hears sounds, it is free from delusion and discrimination;
the nature of the dharma-realm is also thus—discrimination and delusion do not exist therein.
The nose can smell various fragrances, yet its inherent nature is falsely grasped as non-existent;
when both form and characteristics have perished, true emptiness is likewise so.
The self-nature of the tongue-faculty is empty, and it is eternally detached from the realm of flavors.
The nature of consciousness is likewise empty; such is the principle of the dharma-realm.
The self-nature of the body-faculty is pure; sensations of cold and warmth do not exist.
Such too is the principle of the dharma-realm: the locus of touch is eternally transcended.
The mind taking dharmas as its object is said to be supreme; its intrinsic nature is eternally detached.
The nature of all dharmas is fundamentally empty; such is the principle of perfect penetration.
Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—the dharmas associated with them are likewise empty.
To completely sever all deluded thoughts, one realizes that even the principles of seeing and hearing are non-existent.
When the sense organs and their objects give rise to false attachments, the pure essence of the source is lost;
yet, though one is deludedly attached to the existence of organs and objects, in principle, these organs and objects do not exist.
The mundane and the supramundane are, in their emptiness, fundamentally without distinction;
it is through delusion that my [notions of] self and phenomena arise, and through pervasive conceptualization that one wanders in saṃsāra.
The nature of the dharmadhātu is pure and clear; greed, hatred, and ignorance are originally non-existent.
Delusion and awakening arise from the mind; the three poisons are but provisional names.

Deluded attachment binds one to oneself; through the wisdom that realizes these are provisional names, enlightenment is neither near nor far, for the principle of the three periods of time does not exist.
The World-Honored One has proclaimed in the sūtras that the afflictions are a cage of delusive attachments;
when wisdom arises, the defilements of confusion are extinguished—do not let yourself be entangled by false clinging.
Even the most excellent clinging to past and future can be contemplated as empty in its essence.
Awakening is not false attachment; even when correctly realized, it is known to be non-existent.

Just as water and milk are in the same place, yet the swan drinks the milk without mixing it with the water, so too, when birth and emptiness are separated from afflictions, the two obstructions are likewise not mixed.
The deluded attachment that a self exists is not non-existent;
Thoroughly realizing that it is fundamentally non-existent, In the pure principle of Nirvāṇa, Neither of the two selves is established.
Cultivating the three types of giving equally, And observing the precepts free from transgressions and faults.
Patience has the fruit of physical beauty; diligence is the basis for courageous effort;
meditative concentration brings the mind to rest; and wisdom functions without doubt.
May one, combining these with the power of skillful means, abide securely in supreme enlightenment.
Awakening is difficult to falsely grasp; in true emptiness, arising and ceasing do not exist.
When one thoroughly realizes the fundamental nature of emptiness, even these two characteristics are not found to exist.
Just as rock sugar is distinct from sugarcane, it does not exist apart from granulated sugar.
The three vehicles proceed toward enlightenment; Apart from their seeds, their substance does not exist.
By guarding the seed of rice, The sprout and stalk will surely grow.
By guarding the seed of enlightenment, Enlightenment arises from this.
Just as during the dark fortnight, light cannot be seen,
so too when sentient beings are entangled by afflictions, true suchness (tathatā) does not manifest.
Although the moonlight exists at the beginning of the month, it gradually increases.
On the first stage one realizes bodhi, yet bodhi is not yet perfected.
When the moon is full on the fifteenth day, its light is bright and pure everywhere;
liberation manifests the dharmakāya, and the principle of the dharmakāya is without deficiency.
Associated with the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), arising and ceasing together with its fetters,
one is liberated from all obstacles and realizes that the three times are non-existent.
When the first great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is fulfilled, one universally cultivates the three types of giving (*dāna*).
Having severed the obstacles of conceptual discrimination, his joyful wisdom is peerless.
Regarding errors and transgressions of the three karmas, whether grave or light, he guards against them;
with the perfection of śīla, he alone bears the name "Stainless."
The two obstructions, which are perpetually defiling, Are removed by the sword of wisdom that perceives emptiness;
The Ground of Radiance is able to shine forth, Destroying and extinguishing them gradually until nothing remains.
Far removed from the root and secondary defilements, The majesty of the Ground of Blazing Wisdom increases further.
Enlightenment is called supreme; burning and illuminating, it turns ever more radiant.
The ultimate and the conventional are termed the two wisdoms;
when they correspond, they mutually give rise to [insight], and when combined, they are rendered unimpeded—this is the ever-present, invincible task.
The wisdom of the twelvefold dependent origination, with its complete and circular principle, is profound and praised as supreme; thus Prajñā manifests before one.
Having long practiced the paths of the worldly and the two vehicles, one’s cultivation has already become clear.
The signs are perfected without effort; this final stage is called "Far-Reaching.
Its wisdom functions without discrimination, constantly and spontaneously accomplished.
All demons are subdued and dispersed; immovable, it alone bears its name.
Whose excellent wisdom is called "unimpeded," Who rarely expounds the Dharma throughout the ten directions;
Whose cloud-bodies rain down the nectar of immortality, He is most worthy of reliance according to the needs of beings.
His myriad virtues are like water, And his body is likened to space.
Heavy and coarse [afflictions] all obscure and block, While the great Dharma and wisdom are like gathering clouds.
When one scrutinizes the affairs of saṃsāra, Who can escape the pull of karma?
One must know that there is no suffering or affliction; Do not let yourself be entangled in the Pure Land.
I take refuge in the true sons of the Buddha, Who have ascended to the stage of the Cloud of Wisdom;
Having severed all subtle [defilements] to their end, They transcend suffering and leave behind all dust.
The light of the various consecrations shines upon them, Pervading their entire bodies, including the faculties and their objects.
In the Great Samādhi of Vajra-Quiescence, may all sufferings not come near.
Upon the great jewel-flower king-throne, billions of wondrous things are accomplished;
its adornments are everywhere pervasive, and its merit is truly inconceivable.
Possessing the ten powers along with the fearlessnesses, the three bodies and four wisdoms are perfected;
the six supernormal knowledges are ever sovereign, responding to things and transforming according to conditions.
Radiant like the full moon, they blaze with constant, fierce brilliance.
Pervading all ten directions without exception, It blazes forth with ever-fresh radiance.
Forever severed from the defilements born of conditions, It eternally abides in nirvana.
Enlightenment is called supreme; Its transformative benefit gladdens the hearts of beings.
The function of wisdom is as profound as the ocean; it manifests response-bodies according to the capacities of beings.
Just as the moon’s reflection appears when the water is clear, it ferries those lost at the ford across everywhere.
Furthermore, like a crystal gem, it manifests reflections in accordance with conditions, all being identical in nature.
The fundamental nature of things is responsive to stimuli, yet its universal reach is inexhaustible.
Hungry ghosts are perpetually hungry and thirsty, unable to see springs or wells;
sentient beings lack even a slight degree of faith, as their past karma binds them from within.
He manifests the various marks of his physical form, And his radiance shines brilliantly in every direction.
Though the Buddha has always been present in the world, Those with no prior affinity do not behold him.
He clearly understands realms as numerous as dust motes; The afflictions of the faculties have long since ceased.
With the sublime wisdom of the two emptinesses, He employs wondrous skillful means to transform the ignorant and childlike.
Pure and free from all defilements, His bodies of self-enjoyment and enjoyment-for-others Dwell eternally in Akaniṣṭha, Benefiting those of the five vehicles.
He rescues and protects sentient beings from suffering, His lifespan extends for many koṭis of years;
The two adornments are inexhaustible, And his merit is beyond measure.
The Buddha expounds the Dharma of the One Vehicle, Causing awakening according to capacities, whether shallow or deep.
The lotus is unstained by filth; jade is inherently free from the intrusion of flaws.
To praise it even slightly is to proclaim its profound and mysterious principles.
May all these merits bring universal benefit and grace to humans and devas alike.
